eras.name: Warehouses
eras.background: Companies copied data from operational databases into central warehouses for reporting. Parallel databases spread each table over many machines, but they ran as costly appliances that tied storage to compute.

eras.name: Big data
eras.background: Web companies gathered crawls and logs too large to keep in warehouses affordably. Google ran batch jobs on clusters of commodity machines, Hadoop copied the design, and SQL soon returned on top.

eras.name: Low latency
eras.background: Batch jobs were too slow for analysts exploring data and for products reacting to events. Engines moved work into memory and columnar files, and a durable log let stream processors handle events as they arrived.

eras.name: Cloud lakehouse
eras.background: Cloud object stores offered cheap, durable storage, and compute could scale separately from it. Snowflake built a warehouse on them, and open table formats turned lake files into tables that many engines share.

nodes.label: Shared nothing
nodes.problem: The largest databases outgrew single machines, and special database hardware had failed.
nodes.idea: Teradata and Gamma split each table across machines with their own CPU, memory and disks.
nodes.impact: Became the dominant design for data warehouses, though it tied storage to compute.

nodes.label: MapReduce
nodes.problem: Every job over crawled pages and logs had to handle distribution and machine failures itself.
nodes.idea: Users write map and reduce functions; the library spreads the work and reruns failed tasks.
nodes.impact: Its open-source clone, Hadoop, spread batch processing on cheap clusters across industry.

nodes.label: Hive
nodes.idea: Facebook compiles SQL-like queries into MapReduce jobs over tables kept as directories of files.
nodes.impact: SQL returned to big data, and Hive's directory tables became the usual lake layout.

from.why: Every query had to be a custom MapReduce program, hard to maintain and reuse.
Commercial warehouses became too expensive for rapidly growing data.

nodes.label: Dremel
nodes.idea: Google stores nested records column by column and runs SQL through a tree of servers.
nodes.impact: Queries over huge tables returned in seconds, and Dremel came to power BigQuery.

from.why: Ad hoc questions needed chains of MapReduce jobs, far too slow for interactive use.

nodes.label: Kafka
nodes.problem: Log pipelines loaded Hadoop in batches, and message queues could not keep up with activity data.
nodes.idea: LinkedIn stores each topic as partitioned, append-only logs that consumers pull and can rewind.
nodes.impact: Became the common log that feeds both real-time and offline systems.

nodes.label: Spark
nodes.idea: Keep datasets in memory as RDDs and rebuild lost partitions from their lineage.
nodes.impact: Became the most active open-source big data project, with SQL, streaming and machine learning.

from.why: Jobs shared data only by writing it to disk, so iterative and interactive work was slow.

nodes.label: Parquet
nodes.idea: Twitter and Cloudera build an open columnar file format for Hadoop, tied to no engine.
nodes.impact: With ORC, it became one of the two most popular file formats in data lakes.

from.why: Supplied a published way to store nested records column by column.

nodes.label: Presto
nodes.idea: Facebook's engine runs SQL in memory, pipelined across workers, and reads many stores through connectors.
nodes.impact: Interactive SQL on the lake spread to many companies, and Amazon Athena is built on it.

from.why: Hive was tuned for overall throughput, while analysts needed interactive queries with low latency.

nodes.label: Dataflow model
nodes.problem: Events arrive late and out of order, and teams ran separate batch and stream systems.
nodes.idea: Google windows events by when they happened, using watermarks and triggers to decide when to emit.
nodes.impact: Apache Beam implements the model, and Flink adopted many of its techniques.

nodes.label: Flink
nodes.idea: One engine treats batch as bounded streams and checkpoints state with barriers for exactly-once results.
nodes.impact: Made exactly-once stateful stream processing practical at large scale.

from.why: Supplied replayable streams, so a failed job can rewind to its last snapshot.
Supplied the event-time model for handling late, out-of-order events.

nodes.label: Snowflake
nodes.problem: Shared-nothing warehouses tied storage to compute, so resizing a cluster meant reshuffling its data.
nodes.idea: Keep tables in cloud object storage and run queries on separate compute clusters that resize on demand.
nodes.impact: Elastic compute over cloud storage became the norm, and Redshift too moved its data to object storage.

nodes.label: Table formats
nodes.idea: Delta Lake, Iceberg and Hudi record which files form a table in atomically committed metadata.
nodes.impact: Lakes gained ACID updates and time travel, on one copy of data that many engines read.

from.why: Lakes kept Parquet files in Hive-style directories, with no atomic commits and slow listing on object stores.

nodes.label: Lakehouse
nodes.idea: Run warehouse-speed SQL and machine learning directly on open table formats in the lake.
nodes.impact: Snowflake, BigQuery and Redshift now also query Iceberg tables kept in customers' own storage.

from.why: Supplied reliable tables on cheap storage that any engine could read.
Teams still copied lake data into a warehouse, where it was often days stale.

main.why: Every batch job re-solved distribution and failures, so MapReduce lets programmers write map and reduce and leaves the rest to the framework.

main.title: Resilient Distributed Datasets: A Fault-Tolerant Abstraction for In-Memory Cluster Computing
main.why: MapReduce rereads data from disk between iterations, so Spark keeps it in memory as RDDs and rebuilds lost pieces from lineage.

main.title: The Log: What every software engineer should know about real-time data's unifying abstraction
main.why: Point-to-point pipelines between data systems multiply, so one ordered log of changes can feed every database, cache and data system instead.
LinkedIn needed one pipeline for huge volumes of activity data, so Kafka brokers store it as a log that consumers pull at their own pace.
Change capture needs a table's full state and its ongoing changes, so DBLog interleaves chunked dumps with the change stream without locking the table.

main.title: The Dataflow Model
main.why: Events arrive late and out of order, so the Dataflow model handles them with windows, watermarks and triggers.

main.title: Apache Flink: Stream and Batch Processing in a Single Engine
main.why: Separate batch and streaming engines duplicate work, so Flink runs both in one engine, treating batch as a bounded stream.

further.title: Discretized Streams: Fault-Tolerant Streaming Computation at Scale

main.title: State Management in Apache Flink
main.why: Stream jobs hold state that must survive failures, so Flink injects barriers that trigger consistent checkpoints for exactly-once recovery.

background.title: Distributed Snapshots: Determining Global States of Distributed Systems

main.title: Dremel: Interactive Analysis of Web-Scale Datasets
main.why: Interactive queries over nested web data needed columnar storage, so Dremel encodes nested records by column, the scheme Parquet adopted.

further.title: Dremel: A Decade of Interactive SQL Analysis at Web Scale

further.why: Point lookups on a Parquet data lake meant full scans, so Spotify builds an external index that turns each lookup into one small read.

main.title: Major Technical Advancements in Apache Hive
main.why: Hive scanned whole files, so the ORC format stores column statistics that let a query skip data its filter rules out.

main.title: Delta Lake: High-Performance ACID Table Storage over Cloud Object Stores
main.why: Object stores cannot update many files atomically, so Delta Lake keeps a transaction log next to Parquet files for ACID tables.

further.title: Lakehouse: A New Generation of Open Platforms that Unify Data Warehousing and Advanced Analytics

further.why: Hive tables overloaded the metastore and depended on S3 listings, so Airbnb moved ingestion to Iceberg tables and Spark 3.

main.why: Copy-on-write tables rewrite whole files for each update, so Hudi's merge-on-read appends updates to logs and compacts them later.

further.why: Rewriting whole partitions kept Uber's lake data stale, so it built Hudi to apply incremental upserts.

main.why: Each data store needed its own query tool, so Presto runs SQL across many sources through connectors.
Shared-nothing warehouses tie storage to compute, so Snowflake keeps data in S3 and runs queries on separate clusters that scale on their own.

main.title: Druid: A Real-time Analytical Data Store
main.why: Dashboards need fast queries on just-arrived events, so Druid serves fresh data from memory and older data from immutable column segments.

further.title: Pinot: Realtime OLAP for 530 Million Users

main.title: ClickHouse: Lightning Fast Analytics for Everyone
main.why: Real-time analytics needs fast inserts and fast scans, so ClickHouse writes sorted parts, merges them in the background and runs vectorized queries.
